column1: Meanwhile, in the nineteen nineties, China went all in on medicine ingredients.
It built huge plants, in huge drug parks, with cheap power and cheap water.
Its factories also faced looser pollution rules.
And then cheap Chinese penicillin flooded the world market... at prices nobody else could match.
Now remember this one number.
Nineteen ninety-one — the year India opened up its economy.
Of all the medicine powder India bought from outside, China sold less than one per cent.
Less than one.
Then, one by one, the Indian penicillin plants went quiet.
Hindustan Antibiotics.
Stopped.
I.D.P.L.
Stopped.
Torrent.
Ranbaxy.
Sarabhai.
Stopped.
And the last one standing...
Alembic.
Stopped.
By about twenty twenty, India was importing all of that base powder for amoxicillin.
Every last kilo.
Remember that one per cent?
That was for all medicine powder.
Now, if you look at just antibiotic powder today...
China's share is around eighty-six per cent.
Niti Aayog estimates Chinese powder costs thirty-five to forty per cent less than powder made in India.
So tell me — if you ran a company, would you build a plant here?
That's the trap.
You can't compete without a big plant.
And you can't risk a big plant... when one price war can wipe it out.
For years, that trap held.
Then Corona came — and India had to lock its own doors.
And this time, the central government decided to break the trap.
